strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of camera-controlled video generation: relative trajectories do not specify the initial gravity-referenced viewpoint. Gravity-aligned pitch and roll control is useful for cinematic composition, and Section 3 appropriately acknowledges that gravity does not determine absolute yaw.

The combination of panoramic-video resampling and null-pitch captioning is a coherent, practical contribution. Captioning upright views while supervising rotated views directly addresses conflicts between scene descriptions and requested viewing directions. Reusing AC3D’s architecture does not diminish the value of this data-centered approach.

Table 1 reports substantial orientation improvements: pitch error decreases from 41.65 to 23.79 degrees and relative rotation error from 27.81 to 14.25 degrees compared with AC3D plus camera text. The method also outperforms PreciseCam plus WAN on these metrics, and Figure 7 provides supporting qualitative examples.

The null-pitch ablation supports the proposed captioning strategy: pitch error decreases from 28.75 to 23.11 degrees and gravity error from 31.70 to 26.20 degrees. The proposed extreme-viewpoint benchmark addresses a real coverage gap, and the discussion candidly acknowledges translation-sampling limitations and visual artifacts.
weaknesses: The central geometric specification contains consequential ambiguities. Section 3.1 defines the ray direction as R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T + t despite defining t as the camera origin; a direction should exclude this translation. Algorithm 1 samples an initial orientation but never incorporates it into the returned trajectory. Equation 2 also does not transparently implement the stated yaw removal: at the first frame it yields phi(R0)R0, which does not generally preserve the intended pitch and roll under the supplied description of phi. These could be exposition errors rather than implementation failures, but explicit conventions, corrected formulas, and geometric sanity checks are needed to establish reproducibility.

Evaluation relies on unvalidated pose estimators in precisely the extreme-viewpoint regime where estimation can be difficult. Perspective Fields supplies both benchmark selection and generated-video orientation measurements, while VGGT supplies relative motion estimates. Manual filtering of reference videos does not establish estimator accuracy on generated sky, ground, or distorted scenes. Calibration against known panoramic-crop poses, an independent estimator, or human judgments would strengthen confidence that the measured improvements reflect camera control.

The comparisons establish practical gains but incompletely isolate their causes. AC3D is evaluated from its existing checkpoint, and supplying absolute Plücker coordinates to a model trained on relative coordinates is explicitly out of distribution. Beyond the captioning ablation, matched training experiments separating panoramic augmentation, gravity alignment, and trajectory diversity are absent. The current evidence therefore leaves uncertainty about the contribution of each central design choice.

The benchmark and quality assessment need stronger validation. Only 140 reference videos are retained, without uncertainty estimates or clearly reported generation counts. Moreover, their original rotations are discarded when constructing generation conditions, so the reference videos need not match the requested viewpoint distribution. This complicates interpretation of FID/FVD, particularly with such a small reference set. Per-angle results and repeated-seed estimates would also reveal whether aggregate gains persist at the most extreme viewpoints.

The evidence supports improved orientation control more strongly than the broader claims of precise camera manipulation. Mean pitch and gravity errors remain approximately 24 and 27 degrees, translation error does not improve over AC3D, and CLIP and FID are worse than all listed baselines. These tradeoffs do not invalidate the contribution, but ordinary-viewpoint evaluation and a clearer assessment of semantic fidelity would help establish its practical scope. Several implementation and evaluation details are deferred to supplementary material that is not included in the supplied manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation in camera-controlled video generation: relative trajectories do not specify the initial orientation with respect to gravity. Gravity-referenced pitch and roll control has clear value for cinematic shot design.

The panoramic-video pipeline is a useful data-centric contribution. Sampling perspective trajectories from 360-degree videos provides substantially broader orientation coverage while retaining captured scene dynamics. Reusing an existing architecture does not diminish this contribution by itself.

Table 1 reports substantial orientation improvements: pitch error falls from 41.65 to 23.79 degrees and relative rotation error from 27.81 to 14.25 degrees compared with AC3D plus camera text. The qualitative examples support improved viewpoint adherence.

Null-pitch captioning is simple and well motivated. Table 2 provides direct supporting evidence, reducing pitch error from 28.75 to 23.11 degrees while also improving the other reported metrics. The proposed extreme-view benchmark targets an inadequately evaluated capability.
weaknesses: The central geometric specification contains consequential inconsistencies. Section 3.1 adds the camera origin to the ray direction before normalization; under the stated camera-to-world convention, the direction should be proportional to R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T without translation. Equation 2 also does not evidently implement the stated yaw removal: at the first frame it becomes phi(R0)R0, which, under the given definition of phi, doubles a pure pitch rotation. Algorithm 1 samples an initial orientation but never explicitly incorporates it into the returned trajectory. These may be presentation errors, but the supplied manuscript does not establish that the implemented conditioning is geometrically correct.

The comparisons establish an advantage over available pretrained systems but do not adequately isolate the proposed mechanisms. AC3D uses different training data, while the absolute-Plücker baseline receives an out-of-distribution representation without retraining. Matched-data ablations of relative versus gravity-aligned conditioning and restricted versus broad orientation sampling would clarify which changes drive the gains. The null-pitch ablation alone does not resolve this.

The main accuracy evidence depends on unvalidated pose estimators in precisely the difficult regime being studied. Perspective Fields measures generated-image orientation, and VGGT measures relative motion, but their reliability on extreme views, texture-poor sky images, and generated artifacts is not quantified. Manual filtering of benchmark source videos does not validate estimates on generated outputs. Calibration on known-pose panoramic crops or an independent human assessment would strengthen the central conclusions.

The benchmark and statistical reporting leave important uncertainty. Evaluation uses only 140 source videos, with no reported confidence intervals or repeated-seed variability. Reference rotations are discarded and replaced with sampled trajectories, so reference and generated viewpoint distributions are not demonstrated to match for FID/FVD evaluation. The differing full-method results in Tables 1 and 2 are also unexplained. Several necessary protocol and implementation details are deferred to supplementary material unavailable in the supplied manuscript.

The claims of precise control and broad superiority exceed the demonstrated results. Mean pitch and gravity errors remain approximately 24 and 27 degrees, translation error merely ties AC3D, and the method has the lowest CLIP score and highest FID in Table 1; its FVD is also worse than PreciseCam plus WAN. These tradeoffs do not invalidate the orientation contribution, but per-angle results and a clearer analysis of semantic fidelity versus control are needed to establish its practical reliability.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of camera-controlled video generation: relative trajectories do not specify the initial orientation with respect to gravity. Gravity-referenced pitch and roll are useful controls for cinematic composition. Section 3 appropriately clarifies that gravity does not determine absolute yaw.

The main contribution is a practical data and conditioning pipeline. Combining calibrated panoramic videos, varied rotational crops, and gravity-aligned annotations enables broader viewpoint coverage without changing the underlying AC3D architecture. Figure 5 supports the claimed increase in orientation diversity. This is a valuable contribution even without a new network architecture.

Null-pitch captioning is a simple, well-motivated approach to conflicts between scene descriptions and requested viewpoints. Table 2 provides direct supporting evidence: pitch error decreases from 28.75 to 23.11 degrees, gravity error from 31.70 to 26.20 degrees, and relative rotation error from 21.55 to 15.79 degrees.

Table 1 shows substantial orientation improvements over the evaluated alternatives, including the absolute-image-generation-plus-video baseline: pitch error improves from 30.88 to 23.79 degrees and relative rotation error from 24.56 to 14.25 degrees. The qualitative examples support the intended capability. These results give me a slight preference for acceptance, despite the experimental and formulation concerns below.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the benefits of gravity alignment from those of the panoramic training distribution. The absolute-Plücker AC3D baseline changes inputs to a pretrained relative-conditioning model without retraining, which the paper acknowledges is out of distribution. A matched experiment training relative and gravity-aligned conditioning on the same panoramic crops would provide substantially stronger evidence for the representation choice.

The geometric description contains consequential inconsistencies that require clarification. Section 3.1 adds camera translation when computing a ray direction; under the stated camera-origin convention, the direction should be proportional to R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T. Algorithm 1 samples an initial orientation but does not explicitly incorporate it into the returned trajectory. Equation 2 also needs clearer transform conventions and a demonstration that it preserves the desired pitch and roll while removing only the initial yaw. These may be exposition errors, but the supplied manuscript does not establish that.

Evaluation depends heavily on learned pose estimators in precisely the extreme-view regime where their reliability is uncertain. Perspective Fields supplies both benchmark-selection estimates and generated-video orientation measurements; manual filtering of reference videos does not validate its accuracy on generated sky-facing or ground-facing frames. An independent calibration check, angle-stratified results, and uncertainty estimates would strengthen confidence in the reported gains.

SpatialVID-extreme contains only 140 reference videos, and evaluation replaces their rotations with newly sampled trajectories. Consequently, generated and reference viewpoint distributions are not necessarily matched, complicating interpretation of FID/FVD; the small reference set further limits their reliability. No uncertainty is reported, and the differing 'Ours' results in Tables 1 and 2 are unexplained.

The demonstrated capability is improved rather than precise control: mean pitch and gravity errors remain approximately 24 and 27 degrees. The method also has the lowest CLIP score and highest FID in Table 1, while translation accuracy does not improve over AC3D. These tradeoffs merit more analysis. Reproduction is additionally limited by deferring important training, trajectory-sampling, and geometric details to supplementary material that was not supplied.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of camera-controlled video generation: controlling gravity-relative orientation when extreme viewpoints conflict with prompt semantics. The panoramic data pipeline and captioning strategy constitute useful contributions under Algorithms/General, even without a new diffusion architecture.

Null-pitch conditioning is simple, well motivated, and supported by a substantial within-model ablation. In Table 1, it reduces PitchErr from 15.78 to 9.35 degrees and GravityErr from 17.72 to 11.67 degrees. Figure 6 provides complementary evidence that the benefit concentrates at extreme viewpoints.

The full method improves absolute orientation accuracy substantially over UCPE: PitchErr decreases from 16.25 to 9.35 degrees and GravityErr from 18.88 to 11.67 degrees. The qualitative examples also illustrate useful capabilities involving large rotations and initially upward- or downward-facing cameras.

The two proposed benchmarks address gaps in conventional camera-control evaluation. The manuscript identifies its source datasets and pretrained methods, reports training resources, and explicitly acknowledges restricted translation augmentation and visual artifacts.
weaknesses: The central geometric specification needs correction or clarification. Section 3.1 defines the ray direction as RK^{-1}[u,v,1]^T+t, although t is explicitly the camera origin; the direction should exclude that translation. Equation 2 also left-multiplies the pose by a transform described as preserving pitch and roll, without explaining how this removes initial yaw while preserving gravity alignment. These may be presentation errors, but the supplied manuscript does not establish whether the implemented conditioning is geometrically correct.

The experiments do not isolate several central contributions. Baselines use different backbones, and there is no matched training comparison separating gravity alignment, random panoramic trajectory sampling, and the proposed captioning strategy. Feeding absolute poses into an unchanged AC3D checkpoint is a conditioning distribution shift, not a controlled test of absolute versus relative representations. The claim that Plücker representations are inherently ambiguous also confuses the representation with the choice of coordinate frame.

The principal evaluation depends on learned pose estimators whose reliability under the targeted extreme viewpoints is insufficiently established. Perspective Fields supplies training gravity annotations, benchmark selection, and output orientation measurements. Figure 6 includes a useful ground-truth error curve, but a broader calibration or independent validation is missing. VGGT-based relative pose scores likewise lack reported failure rates for large rotations and low-overlap views. With 140 benchmark videos and 20 panorama scenes, uncertainty estimates would help establish robustness.

The broader claim of precise, arbitrary camera control exceeds the demonstrated results. Translation error is 0.72 versus UCPE's 0.44, and the metric normalizes away scale, so it does not validate commands expressed in meters. Null-pitch conditioning also worsens CLIP, FID, and FVD relative to its ablation. Some CLIP reduction is plausibly appropriate, but Figure 6 mean-centers each method's CLIP scores and therefore does not establish comparable absolute semantic fidelity. The orientation-versus-quality tradeoff needs clearer characterization.

Reproducibility and benchmark interpretation remain incomplete in the supplied manuscript. Essential coordinate-transform definitions, training sequence length and batch size, inference settings, and details of the look-down negative prompt are deferred or omitted. Additionally, SpatialVID-extreme replaces reference rotations with independently sampled trajectories, so its reference videos no longer correspond to the requested views; FID/FVD consequently mix visual quality with viewpoint-distribution differences. Together with the geometric and experimental uncertainties, these concerns narrowly outweigh the promising orientation-control results.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation in camera-controlled video generation: specifying gravity-relative orientation and extreme rotations. Under Algorithms/General, its data-generation and captioning contributions are valuable without requiring a new backbone architecture.

The panoramic augmentation pipeline is practical, and null-pitch captioning is a simple, well-motivated way to reduce conflicts between scene descriptions and requested viewpoints. Table 1 provides direct ablation evidence: null-pitch conditioning reduces pitch error from 15.78° to 9.35° and gravity error from 17.72° to 11.67°.

Orientation improvements over the evaluated baselines are substantial: UCPE obtains 16.25° pitch error and 18.88° gravity error. The qualitative examples support improved extreme-viewpoint control, and the two proposed benchmarks target shortcomings of conventional camera-control evaluations.

The manuscript clearly explains the central intuition, attributes its principal data sources and components, and acknowledges restrictions on translation augmentation and visible generation artifacts.
weaknesses: The experiments do not sufficiently isolate the principal contributions. The proposed model uses WAN-2.2, whereas UCPE uses WAN-2.1 and AC3D uses CogVideoX-2B. Beyond null-pitch captioning, there are no controlled ablations separating gravity alignment, panoramic coverage, and trajectory sampling. The AC3D absolute-Plücker variant appears to change conditioning at inference without corresponding retraining, making its poor result weak evidence about the representation.

The geometric formulation requires correction or clarification. Section 3.1 adds camera translation to the ray direction before normalization; under the stated camera-origin convention, the direction should be proportional to R K^-1 [u,v,1]^T without translation. Equation 2 also does not clearly explain how applying a transform described as retaining pitch and roll removes initial yaw while preserving gravity alignment. These could be presentation errors, but the supplied manuscript does not establish that the implemented conditioning is geometrically correct.

Evaluation reliability is insufficiently established for the central extreme-angle claims. Perspective Fields supplies training gravity annotations, benchmark selection estimates, and the principal orientation measurements. Its accuracy on generated images at extreme viewpoints needs independent validation. The 140-video benchmark and 20-scene entanglement benchmark also lack uncertainty estimates. Moreover, benchmark reference rotations are replaced with random conditioning rotations, so FID/FVD compare distributions with potentially different viewpoint statistics.

The broader claim of precise, arbitrary camera control exceeds the evidence. Table 1 reports worse translation error for the proposed method (0.72) than every external baseline (0.40–0.66), and trajectory normalization cannot establish metric translation accuracy despite examples specifying meters. Null-pitch conditioning also worsens FID, FVD, and ordinary CLIP similarity relative to its ablation. These tradeoffs do not negate the orientation gains, but need clearer characterization.

The entanglement analysis provides incomplete evidence of preserved semantics. Figure 6 centers each method's CLIP scores by its own mean, obscuring absolute semantic quality. Correctly generating generic sky or ground at extreme pitch does not establish retention of scene-specific content or consistency when returning to an earlier viewpoint. Absolute scores and quantitative temporal or loop-consistency evaluation would strengthen the scientific case.

Reproduction depends heavily on supplementary details unavailable in the supplied manuscript, including coordinate transforms, camera-encoder specifications, trajectory generation settings, and inference negative prompts. Overall, the orientation improvements make this a close decision, but unresolved geometric and experimental questions support a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of camera-controlled video generation: specifying gravity-relative orientation and maintaining control at extreme viewpoints. Under Algorithms/General, the integrated data and conditioning pipeline is a useful contribution even without a substantially new backbone architecture.

The panorama-based training pipeline provides a practical way to expand orientation coverage while retaining scene motion. Gravity alignment, randomized camera trajectories, and on-the-fly captioning form a coherent approach, with illustrative results demonstrating capabilities beyond conventional forward-facing trajectories.

Null-pitch conditioning is a simple, well-motivated contribution with direct ablation support. In Table 1, it reduces pitch error from 15.78 to 9.35 degrees and gravity error from 17.72 to 11.67 degrees. Against UCPE, the corresponding errors improve from 16.25 and 18.88 degrees, respectively.

The two proposed benchmarks target relevant shortcomings in existing evaluation. The PolyHaven experiment usefully recognizes that ordinary prompt-based CLIP scores can penalize correct camera adherence when requested content lies outside the field of view. The paper also candidly acknowledges restricted translation augmentation and visual artifacts.
weaknesses: The comparisons do not fully isolate the source of improvement. The proposed method uses WAN-2.2 5B, whereas UCPE and other baselines use different backbones and training setups. The null-pitch ablation is informative, but controlled experiments separating gravity alignment, trajectory diversity, and captioning are missing. Supplying absolute Plücker inputs to an unchanged AC3D checkpoint is also not equivalent to training a competitive absolute-pose baseline.

The camera geometry needs correction or clarification. Section 3.1 defines a ray direction as R K^{-1}[u,v,1]^T + t, although t is explicitly the camera origin; the translation should cancel when constructing a direction. Equation 2 also does not clearly explain how its stated pitch/roll-preserving transformation removes initial yaw while preserving gravity alignment. These may be presentation errors, but the implementation must be reconciled with the equations because geometry is central to the contribution.

The evidence supports improved orientation control more strongly than broad, precise camera control. Translation error is 0.72 versus UCPE's 0.44 and 0.62 for two other dynamic baselines. Moreover, trajectory normalization removes scale from evaluation, so metric translation claims, such as moving forward by eight meters, are not validated. Quantitative evidence for full-loop scene consistency is also limited.

Evaluation reliability remains uncertain at the extreme viewpoints that motivate the paper. Perspective Fields is used for training annotations, benchmark selection, and evaluation, while VGGT estimates relative motion from generated frames. Figure 6 provides a useful ground-truth reference curve, but independent validation, estimator failure rates, and uncertainty estimates are absent. The 140-video benchmark and 20-scene entanglement benchmark also limit confidence in small differences.

The quality and semantic tradeoffs deserve clearer analysis. Null-pitch conditioning worsens FID from 108.28 to 115.58 and FVD from 916.83 to 981.0. Figure 6 centers CLIP scores separately for each method, so it establishes variation across pitch rather than superior absolute semantic alignment. Uncentered scores and scene-specific content or human evaluations would help distinguish successful scene-conditioned generation from generic sky/ground outputs.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the supplied manuscript: several camera-transform definitions, architecture details, sampling settings, and negative-prompt construction details are deferred to supplementary material that was not supplied. The benchmark release commitment is welcome, but does not resolve these implementation uncertainties.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful limitation in camera-controlled video generation: specifying gravity-relative pitch and roll, including extreme viewpoints. Under Algorithms/General, the data construction and conditioning strategy constitute a meaningful contribution even though the camera encoders are adopted from existing methods.

The panoramic-video pipeline combines gravity alignment, diverse rotation sampling, and on-the-fly captioning coherently. Demonstrating it with both UCPE and Plücker conditioning across multiple backbones supports its practical applicability.

Null-pitch captioning is a simple, well-motivated contribution. The controlled ablations in Table 1 support its effectiveness: pitch error decreases from 18.92 to 13.98 degrees with UCPE and from 14.39 to 8.36 degrees with WAN-2.2/Plücker. Figure 6 further examines the intended prompt–camera conflict.

The quantitative improvements in absolute orientation are substantial for several configurations. For example, the CogVideoX variant reduces pitch error from 39.09 to 21.19 degrees, while the WAN-2.1/Plücker variant reduces it from 29.16 to 10.50 degrees. Qualitative examples provide additional evidence of improved extreme-viewpoint handling.

The proposed benchmarks target an underexplored evaluation setting. The paper also appropriately explains why ordinary prompt-based CLIP scores can penalize correct camera control, acknowledges translation augmentation and visual-artifact limitations, and clarifies that its absolute reference fixes pitch and roll rather than global yaw.
weaknesses: The central orientation evaluation needs stronger independent validation. Perspective Fields supplies training gravity annotations, selects the extreme-pitch benchmark, and measures generated orientation. This creates shared estimator dependence, particularly for sky/ground images where orientation may be ambiguous. Figure 6 includes a useful ground-truth curve, but the paper does not systematically establish estimator accuracy across extreme pitch and roll, or report VGGT failure handling for large rotations and limited overlap.

The closest prior work, UCPE, already combines panoramic data with gravity-aware conditioning. The clearest novelty is therefore trajectory sampling and caption construction, rather than gravity-aware control itself. A matched comparison isolating the proposed sampling from UCPE's sampling is missing. Notably, the proposed UCPE pipeline without null-pitch conditioning has worse absolute orientation errors than original UCPE, although it improves relative rotation.

The visual-quality evidence is limited and the tradeoff deserves more explicit treatment. SpatialVID-extreme contains only 138 reference videos, with no uncertainty estimates for FID/FVD. Its reference rotations are also replaced when constructing generation inputs, weakening conditional comparability. WAN-2.1/Plücker improves orientation but worsens FVD from 776.3 to 1041.6; adding null-pitch conditioning to WAN-2.2 worsens FVD from 895.2 to 1014.4.

Broad claims of precise, arbitrary camera control exceed the demonstrated evidence. Translation errors are generally worse than corresponding baselines, and trajectory normalization prevents verification of metric translation commands such as the eight-meter example in Figure 1. Full-turn scene consistency and dynamic-content preservation are illustrated rather than systematically measured.

The entanglement benchmark contains only 20 independent scenes, despite its 380 prompt-angle pairs. It primarily measures static pitch control and does not establish robustness for joint extreme pitch/roll trajectories. Angle-specific reference captions improve the relevance of CLIP evaluation, but cannot alone show that generated off-screen content remains consistent with the requested scene.

Reproduction from the supplied manuscript is incomplete. Important training settings, filtering thresholds, negative-prompt details, and coordinate functions are deferred to unavailable supplementary material. Equation 4 particularly needs explicit transform conventions and definitions of its yaw-removal operation to verify gravity preservation. These gaps limit verification of the implementation, although they do not by themselves demonstrate that it is incorrect.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation in controllable video generation: specifying gravity-relative orientation and maintaining control at extreme viewpoints. Under Algorithms/General, the data construction and conditioning strategy constitute a useful contribution even though the camera encoders are inherited from prior work.

Null-pitch captioning is a simple, well-motivated intervention for prompt–camera conflicts. Its ablation supports its effectiveness across two model configurations: pitch error falls from 18.92° to 13.98° with WAN 2.1/UCPE and from 14.39° to 8.36° with WAN 2.2/Plücker conditioning.

The framework is demonstrated across multiple backbones and conditioning mechanisms. Against UCPE on the same backbone, Table 1 improves pitch error from 16.25° to 13.98° and relative rotation error from 18.38° to 12.12°. These results provide evidence beyond selected qualitative examples.

The two proposed evaluations target relevant gaps in existing benchmarks. The paper also appropriately recognizes that ordinary prompt–video CLIP similarity can penalize correct camera adherence, and its angle-specific caption evaluation provides a useful complementary diagnostic. The acknowledged translation and visual-artifact limitations are constructive.
weaknesses: The novelty should be positioned more narrowly against UCPE, which already combines gravity-aware conditioning with panoramic training data. The strongest distinctions are trajectory sampling and caption construction, rather than absolute camera control itself. A controlled comparison with UCPE-style trajectory sampling under matched data and training would better establish the sampling contribution; removing absolute rotations mostly confirms the expected consequence of withholding the target orientation.

Camera accuracy depends heavily on unvalidated estimator behavior at the very viewpoints emphasized by the paper. Perspective Fields supplies training gravity annotations, benchmark selection, and absolute-orientation evaluation. This reuse does not invalidate the results, but independent calibration or manual verification is needed, particularly for ambiguous sky/ground views. VGGT-based relative pose evaluation likewise needs failure-rate reporting for large rotations, low overlap, and dynamic scenes.

The evaluation is small and incompletely supports the broad motion claims. SpatialVID-extreme contains 138 reference videos, while the entanglement benchmark contains only 20 distinct panoramas evaluated at static pitches. Aggregate errors do not establish reliable full-turn closure, scene preservation on revisiting a view, or performance across rotation amplitudes. Figure 2 is encouraging, but these capabilities need systematic measurement and uncertainty estimates.

Orientation gains come with material tradeoffs. With WAN 2.1/Plücker, FVD worsens from 776.3 for PreciseCam+WAN to 1041.6, and translation error rises from 0.62 to 0.68. On WAN 2.2, adding null-pitch conditioning worsens FVD from 895.2 to 1014.4. Moreover, benchmark input rotations replace the reference videos’ rotations, so FID/FVD can reflect viewpoint-distribution mismatch as well as quality. The paper should distinguish these effects before claiming broadly competitive visual quality.

Several details needed to verify the geometric pipeline and reproduce training are deferred to supplementary material unavailable in the supplied manuscript. Equation 4 needs explicit coordinate conventions and definitions of its transformations: the stated pitch/roll-preserving function and its left multiplication do not transparently explain yaw removal. Training schedules, filtering thresholds, and how poses from the six perspective streams are combined also require specification. Finally, normalized translation evaluation does not substantiate metric-distance control such as the '8 meters' example in Figure 1.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful limitation of camera-controlled video generation: controlling orientation relative to gravity, particularly at extreme pitch and roll. Under the default Algorithms/General category, the data construction and conditioning strategy constitute a useful contribution despite reusing existing camera encoders.

The combination of calibrated panoramic videos, randomized rotation trajectories, and null-pitch captioning is coherent and practically motivated. Null-pitch captioning offers a simple way to reduce conflicts between scene descriptions and camera orientation.

Table 1 demonstrates improvements across multiple backbones and both Plücker and UCPE encodings. On the matched UCPE architecture, pitch error decreases from 16.25 to 13.98 degrees and relative rotation error from 18.38 to 12.12 degrees. The larger orientation improvements on the Plücker variants further support the approach's applicability.

The null-pitch ablations substantiate a central design choice: removing it increases pitch error from 8.36 to 14.39 degrees on WAN 2.2 and from 13.98 to 18.92 degrees on the UCPE variant. The separate prompt-camera experiment provides complementary evidence.

The proposed benchmarks target capabilities inadequately measured by conventional forward-facing video datasets. The manuscript also appropriately clarifies that absolute orientation refers to gravity-aligned pitch and roll, distinguishes static-scene baselines, and acknowledges translation-augmentation limitations and visual artifacts.
weaknesses: The evaluation is relatively small: SpatialVID-extreme contains 138 reference videos, and the entanglement benchmark contains only 20 independent scenes. No confidence intervals or repeated-run variability are reported. This particularly limits confidence in modest improvements over UCPE and comparisons using FID/FVD.

Orientation evaluation relies on Perspective Fields, which also supplies training gravity annotations and benchmark selection estimates. Its reliability on generated imagery and extreme viewpoints needs stronger independent validation. VGGT-based trajectory measurements likewise need failure-rate reporting for large rotations with little overlap; Figure 6's ground-truth curve is useful but does not fully establish measurement reliability.

Improved orientation control comes with measurable tradeoffs. For WAN 2.1 with Plücker conditioning, FVD worsens from 776.3 to 1041.6 and translation error from 0.62 to 0.68 relative to PreciseCam+WAN. Null-pitch conditioning also worsens WAN 2.2 FVD from 895.2 to 1014.4. The discussion should distinguish these quality costs from the reasonably justified reduction in ordinary prompt CLIP score.

The incremental contribution over UCPE needs sharper isolation. UCPE already uses panoramic data and gravity-aware conditioning; the new contribution is primarily trajectory sampling and caption construction. The supplied experiments do not independently isolate the sampling policy under matched training data and compute, and broad claims of previously unavailable extreme-rotation capabilities exceed the aggregate quantitative evidence.

Some central implementation details are deferred to supplementary material unavailable in the supplied PDF, including training schedules, filtering thresholds, and precise coordinate transforms. Equation 4 especially needs clarification: the described roll/pitch-preserving operator is left-multiplied into the pose, yet is claimed to establish zero initial yaw while preserving gravity alignment. Explicit frame conventions and a derivation would make this reproducible and verifiable.
